title: Green helps
hookLine: a 2015 Stanford study found a nature walk reduced brooding compared to a city walk (Bratman et al.)
carry: take it for a walk somewhere green

lines: A BUSY ROAD, OR THE OAKS.
cards: You know the loop. Something someone said at lunch, and your mind keeps chewing on it. What I should have said.
What they meant. Why this always happens to me. Psychologists call that loop rumination, the same word used for a cow chewing its cud, and it's one of the things most tied to low mood.
Now two walks. One along a busy road, four lanes of traffic, shops and noise. One on a quiet path through grassland and old oak trees.
Same length, same pace. In 2015 researchers at Stanford sent people on one or the other, then asked how much they were still chewing.

teach.b: Gregory Bratman and his colleagues sent healthy city dwellers on a ninety-minute walk: half in green parkland near the Stanford campus, half beside a busy multi-lane road in Palo Alto.
Before and after, they filled out a questionnaire about brooding and had their brains scanned.
The nature walkers reported less rumination afterward, and showed less activity in the subgenual prefrontal cortex, a brain area linked to that kind of looping, negative self-focus.

teach.h: THE OAKS QUIETED IT; THE ROAD DIDN'T.
teach.b: The city walkers didn't show the change. It was a small study, about forty people, one piece of a larger pattern, not the last word.
Many studies link time in green places with lower stress and better mood, though cause is hard to untangle: people with more free time and money often live nearer parks. Remember: compared to what.
In Japan, in the 1980s, the forestry agency began promoting shinrin-yoku, forest bathing: not hiking or exercise, just being among trees, slowly, with all your senses.
And in Concord, Henry David Thoreau, who went to the woods to live deliberately, wrote an essay called Walking.

He claimed he couldn't keep his health and spirits without hours every day spent "sauntering through the woods and over the hills and fields, absolutely free from all worldly engagements." Four hours is a lot.
The Stanford walkers had ninety minutes. But the direction is the same. When the loop won't stop, you don't have to out-argue it.
You can take it for a walk somewhere green.

how: Many people take regular walks in parks or woods to clear their heads; in Japan, shinrin-yoku, forest bathing, means spending slow, unhurried time among trees.

o: the color green calms people in any setting
time among trees can quiet a brooding mind
houseplants clean the air you breathe at home

games.q: the walk study — tap the pairs.

s: in the 2015 study, the nature walkers reported less brooding
and showed less activity in a brain area linked to it; the road walkers didn't.
forest bathing means swimming in a forest lake
it means slow time among trees, with all your senses.
studies prove parks cause better mood
the link is consistent, but cause is hard to untangle; people near parks differ in other ways.

games.q: you can't stop replaying a hard conversation. you have ninety minutes free. what did the Stanford study test?
games.why: the green walkers reported less rumination afterward. the traffic walkers didn't.

practice: Rest your eyes on something green: a tree outside the window, a park, a houseplant, even a picture of a forest. Pick out every shade of green you can see, and notice movement, leaves, light.
If a thought starts chewing, let it, and bring your eyes back to the green.

wordCard.voice: Green helps. In one study, a walk among trees quieted brooding in a way a walk beside traffic didn't.

orig.note: Japanese: forest bathing; a term promoted by Japan's forestry agency in the 1980s.

carryVoice: Your line: take it for a walk somewhere green. The loop can come along. Day three hundred seventeen.
